young.html: When you see a sunset and say "That's beautiful!", what are you saying? Are you saying something about the sunset, or about you? Immanuel Kant wrote a book about this.

Kant noticed that liking candy is different from finding a flower beautiful. If you like candy and I don't, fine: tastes differ. But when you call a flower beautiful, you speak as if everyone ought to agree, even though you can't prove it with reasons.

Kant also wrote about the sublime: things so huge or powerful, like a storm at sea, a towering mountain or the night sky, that they almost overwhelm us. From a safe place, they make us feel small and yet strangely great, because our minds can think of something even bigger: the infinite.

young.html: Beauty walk. Go outside and each find one thing you think is beautiful. Bring it back or describe it. Can you give a reason why others should find it beautiful too? Is that easy or hard? Then look up at the clouds or the night sky. Does anything feel "sublime"?

full.html: Kant's first Critique was about knowledge of nature; his second, about morality and freedom. The Critique of Judgment (1790) tries to bridge them through the power of judgment: fitting particular things under general ideas. It has two parts: judgments of taste (the beautiful and the sublime) and judgments of purpose in nature, especially in living things.

Kant analyzes the judgment "this is beautiful" in four "moments." It is disinterested: the pleasure doesn't depend on wanting to own or use the thing. It claims universal agreement. It finds in the object a purposiveness without purpose: it seems designed, but for no purpose we can name. And its claim is necessary, resting on a sense we all share.

full.text: The beautiful is that which pleases universally, without a concept.

full.html: Kant distinguishes the mathematically sublime, the vastly great, such as the starry sky or the pyramids seen up close, which our imagination can't take in at one glance, and the dynamically sublime, overwhelming power such as storms, volcanoes and waterfalls, which we find sublime only when we are safe. Either way, he says, the feeling points to something in us: reason's idea of the infinite and our moral freedom, which no force of nature can master.

full.name: gb-beauty-sublime
full.cap: Slide from small and gentle to vast and powerful. Where does the beautiful end and the sublime begin?

full.html: Fine art, Kant says, must look as free as nature, and it is the work of genius, a talent that gives the rule to art rather than following rules. In the second part he argues that living things seem to us to be organized for purposes: each part exists for the whole and the whole for the parts, as a tree makes its own leaves. We can't explain this by mechanism alone, he thought, so we must judge living things as if they were designed, while knowing that this is a guide for our inquiry, not proof of a designer.
Thinking Kant said beauty is just personal taste. He said the opposite of the pleasant: a judgment of beauty claims everyone's agreement, though it can't be proved by rules or concepts.

deep.html: The Critique of Judgment became a founding book of modern aesthetics. The Romantic poets and painters took up the sublime (the Art Ladder's rung on Romanticism shows paintings of storms and mountains). Schiller built a theory of education on Kant's idea of free play. In biology, Kant's remark that it is absurd to hope "another Newton will arise" who could explain a blade of grass living things by mechanical laws alone was later challenged by Darwin's theory of natural selection, which explains the appearance of design without a designer; that debate continues in the next era.
